chapter_title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

questions.text: A person suffering from myopia cannot see distant objects clearly. Which type of corrective lens should be prescribed?

key_points: In myopia image forms in front of retina
Concave lens diverges rays so image shifts back onto retina
rubric.expected_answer: Concave (diverging) lens. In myopia the far point is nearer than infinity; a concave lens of suitable negative power brings the image of a distant object onto the retina.
rubric.hint: Think about which lens type pushes the image back onto the retina for myopia.

questions.text: A student sitting at the back of the classroom cannot read the text on the blackboard but can read her textbook clearly. Which defect of vision is she most likely suffering from?

key_points: Cannot see distant objects
Can see nearby objects — hallmark of myopia
rubric.expected_answer: Myopia (near-sightedness). The student sees nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects.
rubric.hint: Clear near vision but blurred distant vision is the hallmark of which defect?

questions.text: State two causes of myopia. How can this defect be corrected? Name the type and sign of power of the corrective lens.

key_points: Cause 1: excessive curvature of the eye lens
Cause 2: elongation of the eyeball
Correction: concave lens, negative power
rubric.expected_answer: Causes: (i) Excessive curvature of the crystalline lens. (ii) Elongation of the eyeball. Correction: A concave (diverging) lens of suitable negative power is used to diverge incoming parallel rays so they converge onto the retina.
rubric.hint: State causes (lens curvature or eyeball length) and which lens type diverges the light.

questions.text: Distinguish between myopia and hypermetropia with respect to: (a) which objects are seen clearly, (b) where the image forms in the uncorrected eye, (c) the type of corrective lens used.

key_points: Myopia: nearby clear; distant blurred; image in front of retina; concave lens
Hypermetropia: distant clear; nearby blurred; image behind retina; convex lens
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Myopia: nearby clear, distant blurred. Hypermetropia: distant clear, nearby blurred. (b) Myopia: image in front of retina. Hypermetropia: image behind retina. (c) Myopia: concave lens. Hypermetropia: convex lens.
rubric.hint: Compare where each defect forms the image (front vs behind retina) and which lens corrects each.

questions.text: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. Find the nature and power of the lens required to correct this defect.

key_points: v = -0.8 m (far point), u = -infinity
P = -1.25 D; concave lens
rubric.expected_answer: Far point = 80 cm = 0.8 m. Corrective lens must form image of distant object (u = -inf) at far point: v = -0.8 m. 1/f = 1/(-0.8) - 0 = -1.25 m^-1. Power P = -1.25 D. Nature: concave (diverging) lens.
rubric.hint: Use u = -infinity, v = -far_point in metres, then P = 1/v - 1/u.

questions.text: The near point of a hypermetropic person is 1 m. What is the power of the corrective lens required? (Assume normal near point = 25 cm.)

key_points: P = +3.0 D; convex lens
rubric.expected_answer: u = -0.25 m (object at normal near point), v = -1.0 m (virtual image at hypermetropic near point). 1/f = 1/(-1.0) - 1/(-0.25) = -1 + 4 = +3.0 D. Power = +3.0 D. Nature: convex (converging) lens.
rubric.hint: Use u = -0.25 m (normal near point) and v = -near_point in metres, then P = 1/v - 1/u.

questions.text: A person requires a lens of power -5.5 dioptres for correcting distant vision and +1.5 dioptres for near vision. Calculate the focal length of the lens required for (i) distant vision and (ii) near vision.

key_points: f = 1/P
rubric.expected_answer: (i) Distant: P = -5.5 D. f = 1/(-5.5) = -0.18 m = -18 cm. Concave lens. (ii) Near: P = +1.5 D. f = 1/(1.5) = +0.67 m = +67 cm. Convex lens.
rubric.hint: Apply f = 1/P for each power value and convert to cm if needed.

questions.text: What is presbyopia? State its two causes. Explain how it is corrected. How does it differ from hypermetropia?

key_points: Definition: age-related loss of accommodation
Cause 1: weakening of ciliary muscles
Cause 2: diminishing flexibility of crystalline lens
Correction: bifocal lenses
Difference: hypermetropia is structural (any age); presbyopia is age-related loss of flexibility
rubric.expected_answer: Presbyopia: gradual decrease in power of accommodation with ageing, making it difficult to see nearby objects. Causes: (1) Weakening of ciliary muscles. (2) Diminishing flexibility of crystalline lens. Correction: Bifocal lenses — upper concave portion for distant vision, lower convex portion for near vision. Difference from hypermetropia: Hypermetropia is a structural refractive defect (eyeball too small or lens focal length too long) that can occur at any age; presbyopia is specifically due to age-related loss of lens flexibility and ciliary muscle weakness.
rubric.hint: Focus on age-related loss of accommodation due to ciliary muscles and lens flexibility.

questions.text:
(a) Draw labeled ray diagrams showing (i) the defect of hypermetropia and (ii) its correction using a suitable lens.
(b) A person cannot see objects placed closer than 1.5 m. Find the power of corrective lens. (Normal near point = 25 cm.)

key_points: Diagram: image behind retina in hypermetropic eye; convex lens corrects
rubric.expected_answer: (a)(i) Rays converge behind retina in hypermetropic eye. (ii) Convex lens in front brings image forward onto retina. (b) u = -0.25 m, v = -1.5 m. P = 1/(-1.5) - 1/(-0.25) = +3.33 D. Convex lens of power +3.33 D.
rubric.hint: For diagram show image behind retina; for calculation use P = 1/v - 1/u with correct signs.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): A person suffering from both myopia and hypermetropia is prescribed bifocal lenses.
Reason (R): The upper portion of a bifocal lens is concave and the lower portion is convex.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: A true: bifocal for both defects
R true: upper concave (distant), lower convex (near)
R explains A
rubric.expected_answer: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A. Upper concave corrects myopia; lower convex corrects hypermetropia.
rubric.hint: Think about which lens goes on top (distant) and which on bottom (near) in bifocal lenses.

questions.text: The human eye forms the image of an object at its

key_points: Retina is the light-sensitive screen; image is formed here
rubric.expected_answer: Retina. The eye lens system forms a real, inverted image on the retina.
rubric.hint: Think about which eye structure contains light-sensitive rods and cones.

questions.text: Which part of the human eye controls the size of the pupil to regulate the amount of light entering the eye?

key_points: Iris is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil
rubric.expected_answer: Iris. The iris is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil, regulating light entering the eye.
rubric.hint: Think about which structure acts as a muscular diaphragm controlling the size of the pupil.

questions.text: State the function of each of the following parts of the human eye: (a) Cornea (b) Iris (c) Crystalline lens (d) Retina.

key_points: Cornea: most refraction
Iris: controls pupil
Crystalline lens: accommodation
Retina: light to electrical signals
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Cornea: transparent front membrane; provides most of the refraction. (b) Iris: muscular diaphragm; controls pupil size to regulate light. (c) Crystalline lens: adjusts focal length via ciliary muscles (accommodation). (d) Retina: light-sensitive; rods and cones generate electrical signals sent via optic nerve to brain.
rubric.hint: For each part, think: does it refract, regulate light, adjust focal length, or convert signals?

questions.text: Describe the structure of the human eye with the help of a labeled diagram. Explain how an image is formed on the retina.

key_points: Spherical eyeball ~2.3 cm
Cornea: most refraction
Iris+Pupil: regulate light
Crystalline lens+ciliary muscles: accommodation
Retina: rods and cones, electrical signals
Optic nerve: to brain
Image: real, inverted on retina
rubric.expected_answer: The eyeball is spherical (~2.3 cm diameter). Cornea: transparent front; most refraction. Iris: muscular diaphragm; controls pupil. Crystalline lens: converging; ciliary muscles change its curvature. Aqueous humour (front) and vitreous humour (back) are fluids. Retina: light-sensitive; rods (dim light) and cones (colour) produce electrical signals. Optic nerve: transmits signals to brain. Image: light refracts at cornea and lens; forms real, inverted image on retina; brain interprets as upright.
rubric.hint: Describe each component from cornea to optic nerve; image on retina is real and inverted.

questions.text: In what ways is the human eye similar to a camera? State two important differences between the two in terms of focus adjustment and image recording.

key_points: Similarity 1: both form real inverted image using converging lens
Similarity 2: both have aperture to regulate light
Difference 1: camera fixed focal length; eye adjusts by accommodation
Difference 2: camera records on film/sensor; eye uses living retina
rubric.expected_answer: Similarities: (1) Both use a converging lens to form a real, inverted image. (2) Both have an adjustable aperture (camera diaphragm vs. iris and pupil). Differences: (1) A camera lens has a fixed focal length; the human eye adjusts its focal length via accommodation (ciliary muscles). (2) A camera records on film or electronic sensor; the human eye uses a living retina that sends electrical signals to the brain.
rubric.hint: Compare focus adjustment: camera moves lens mechanically; eye changes lens shape by accommodation.

questions.text: The change in focal length of the crystalline lens of the human eye is caused by the action of the

key_points: Ciliary muscles change lens curvature and hence focal length
rubric.expected_answer: Ciliary muscles. Contraction increases curvature (shorter focal length); relaxation decreases curvature (longer focal length).
rubric.hint: Think about which muscle changes the curvature of the crystalline lens.

questions.text: What is meant by the power of accommodation of the human eye? State the near point and far point of a normal human eye.

key_points: Power of accommodation: ability to adjust focal length
Near point = 25 cm
Far point = infinity
rubric.expected_answer: Power of accommodation: the ability of the crystalline lens to adjust its focal length (via ciliary muscles) so objects at different distances are clearly seen on the retina. Near point of normal eye = 25 cm. Far point of normal eye = infinity.
rubric.hint: Define accommodation and state both the near point and far point of a normal eye.

questions.text: Describe the changes in (a) ciliary muscles, (b) curvature of the eye lens, and (c) focal length of the eye lens, when you shift your gaze from a distant object to a nearby object.

key_points: (a) Ciliary muscles contract
(b) Curvature increases — lens thickens
(c) Focal length decreases — enables near vision
rubric.expected_answer: When shifting from distant to nearby: (a) Ciliary muscles contract. (b) Curvature of lens increases — lens becomes thicker and more convex. (c) Focal length decreases. The greater converging power focuses the nearby object's diverging rays onto the retina.
rubric.hint: Ciliary muscles contract for near vision; what happens to curvature and focal length?

questions.text: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly objects placed closer than 25 cm? What would happen if you tried to read text held just 5 cm from your eyes?

key_points: Focal length cannot decrease below minimum even with full contraction
At < 25 cm image falls behind retina causing blur
Eye strain results from excessive effort
rubric.expected_answer: The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a minimum limit even with full ciliary muscle contraction. For objects closer than 25 cm, the required focal length is smaller than this minimum; the image forms behind the retina producing a blurred image and eye strain. At 5 cm: the image would be severely blurred and significant eye strain would result.
rubric.hint: Think about the minimum focal length limit even with full ciliary muscle contraction.

questions.text: When white light passes through a triangular glass prism, which colour is deviated the most and which is deviated the least?

key_points: Violet: shortest wavelength — most deviation
Red: longest wavelength — least deviation
rubric.expected_answer: Most deviated: Violet (shortest wavelength). Least deviated: Red (longest wavelength).
rubric.hint: Relate deviation to wavelength: shorter wavelength gives more or less deviation in a prism?

questions.text: What is dispersion of light? Write the full sequence of colours in the visible spectrum and give the acronym. Which scientist first demonstrated this with sunlight?

key_points: Dispersion: splitting of white light into component colours
VIBGYOR: Violet Indigo Blue Green Yellow Orange Red
Isaac Newton first demonstrated this
rubric.expected_answer: Dispersion: splitting of white light into its component colours by a glass prism. Spectrum colours: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red — acronym VIBGYOR (violet most deviated, red least). First demonstrated by Isaac Newton.
rubric.hint: Name the splitting phenomenon, recall VIBGYOR order, and who first demonstrated it with sunlight.

questions.text: State two conditions necessary to observe a rainbow. Explain the role of water droplets in rainbow formation with the help of a diagram.

key_points: Condition 1: sunlight must be present
Condition 2: rain/water droplets in atmosphere; observer with sun behind
Droplet: refracts+disperses on entry, total internal reflection, refracts on exit
rubric.expected_answer: Conditions: (1) Bright sunlight. (2) Rain or water droplets in atmosphere opposite to the Sun from the observer. Role of droplets: Each raindrop acts as a tiny prism — sunlight refracts and disperses on entering, undergoes internal reflection inside, refracts again on exiting. Different colours emerge at different angles, creating the rainbow arc.
rubric.hint: Two conditions: sunlight present and raindrops opposite Sun; each droplet acts like a prism.

questions.text: Describe Newton's experiment to show that sunlight consists of seven colours. What did he observe when a second identical prism was placed in an inverted position? What conclusion did he draw?

key_points: First prism: white light splits into VIBGYOR
Tried splitting colours further — could not
Second inverted prism: all colours recombined into white light
Conclusion: white light made of seven colours
rubric.expected_answer: Experiment: Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and obtained a VIBGYOR spectrum. He tried to split individual colours with another prism but could not. He then placed a second identical prism in an inverted position; all spectrum colours passed through it and a beam of white light emerged from the other side. Conclusion: sunlight (white light) is composed of seven colour components that can be separated (dispersion) and recombined. Any light giving this spectrum is called white light.
rubric.hint: First prism splits; second inverted prism recombines all colours — what does this prove?

questions.text: Draw a labeled diagram showing the dispersion of white light by a glass prism. Identify which colour suffers (a) maximum deviation and (b) minimum deviation. Name the acronym for the sequence of colours.

key_points: Diagram: prism with white light in, VIBGYOR out
Violet: max deviation; Red: min deviation
Acronym: VIBGYOR
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram: triangular prism with white light beam incident on one face; VIBGYOR emerging from second face (violet most deviated, red least). (a) Maximum deviation: Violet. (b) Minimum deviation: Red. Acronym: VIBGYOR.
rubric.hint: Draw prism with white light in and VIBGYOR out; violet deviates most, red deviates least.

questions.text: The angle between the direction of the incident ray and the direction of the emergent ray after passing through a triangular glass prism is called the

key_points: Angle of deviation (angle D) is between incident ray direction and emergent ray direction
rubric.expected_answer: Angle of deviation (angle D). It is the angle through which the incident ray is deflected by the prism.
rubric.hint: The angle between the incident ray direction and emergent ray direction has a specific name.

questions.text: A ray of light passes through a triangular glass prism. (a) Why is the emergent ray not parallel to the incident ray? (b) How is this different from what happens in a rectangular glass slab?

key_points: Prism: inclined surfaces; both refractions deviate in same direction; angle of deviation
Slab: parallel surfaces; refractions cancel; emergent ray parallel, only lateral displacement
rubric.expected_answer: (a) The two refracting surfaces of a prism are inclined to each other. At each surface the ray bends in the same direction; the cumulative bending produces an angle of deviation between incident and emergent rays. (b) In a glass slab the surfaces are parallel; bending at surface 1 is reversed at surface 2; emergent ray is parallel to incident ray (only lateral displacement occurs).
rubric.hint: Inclined surfaces in prism add deviation; parallel surfaces in slab cancel out deviation.

questions.text: Draw a labeled diagram showing the refraction of light through a triangular glass prism. Label: incident ray (PE), refracted ray (EF), emergent ray (FS), angle of incidence (i), angle of refraction (r), angle of emergence (e), angle of prism (A), and angle of deviation (D).

key_points: Prism ABC; ray PE on AB; refracted EF; emergent FS from AC
Normals at E and F
All five angles correctly marked
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram: triangular prism with apex A. Incident ray PE on face AB at E; refracted ray EF inside prism; emergent ray FS exiting face AC at F. Normals at E and F. Angle i (incident with normal at E), r (refracted with normal at E), e (emergent with normal at F), A (prism apex), D (between extended PE direction and FS direction).
rubric.hint: Draw triangular prism with all five angles (i, r, e, A, D) and all three rays labelled.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): When a ray of light passes through a glass prism, the emergent ray is not parallel to the incident ray.
Reason (R): The two refracting surfaces of a prism are inclined to each other (not parallel).

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: A true: angle of deviation exists
R true: non-parallel surfaces
R explains A: inclined surfaces cause both refractions to add — angle of deviation
rubric.expected_answer: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A. The inclined surfaces cause both refractions to deviate the ray in the same direction, resulting in the angle of deviation.
rubric.hint: Check whether inclined surfaces correctly explain why emergent ray is not parallel to incident.

questions.text: The twinkling of stars is due to

options.text: Scattering of starlight by atmospheric dust
Dispersion of starlight by water vapour

key_points: Twinkling is due to atmospheric refraction
rubric.expected_answer: Atmospheric refraction of starlight. The continuously changing refractive index of the atmosphere causes the apparent position to fluctuate, making starlight entering the eye flicker.
rubric.hint: Think about which atmospheric property changes continuously and bends starlight.

questions.text: Stars twinkle but planets do not. Give a scientific explanation for this difference.

key_points: Stars: point sources; atmospheric refraction causes fluctuating light — twinkling
Planets: extended sources; individual point fluctuations average to zero — no twinkling
rubric.expected_answer: Stars are very far away and appear as point-sized sources. Atmospheric refraction causes their apparent position to fluctuate; the amount of light reaching the eye flickers — twinkling. Planets are closer and appear as extended sources (collection of many point sources); individual fluctuations average to zero — no twinkling.
rubric.hint: Stars are point sources; planets are extended sources — how does size affect light fluctuations?

questions.text: Explain how atmospheric refraction causes (a) advance sunrise and (b) delayed sunset. By approximately how many minutes does each occur?

key_points: Atmosphere bends light towards normal
Apparent position of Sun above actual position near horizon
Sun visible ~2 min before actual sunrise and ~2 min after actual sunset
rubric.expected_answer: The atmosphere has increasing refractive index towards the Earth's surface. It bends the Sun's light towards the normal, making the apparent position slightly above the actual position near the horizon. (a) Advance sunrise: Sun visible ~2 minutes before it actually crosses the horizon. (b) Delayed sunset: Sun visible ~2 minutes after it has actually set. Atmospheric refraction also causes flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise/sunset.
rubric.hint: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight upward near horizon; by approximately how many minutes?

questions.text: Explain in detail the phenomenon of twinkling of stars due to atmospheric refraction. Why does the apparent position of a star differ from its actual position? Why do planets not show this effect?

key_points: Atmosphere: gradually changing refractive index
Continuous refraction bends starlight — apparent position above actual
Changing conditions — apparent position keeps shifting
Stars are point sources — light flickers — twinkling
Planets extended sources — variations average to zero — no twinkling
rubric.expected_answer: The Earth's atmosphere has a medium of gradually increasing refractive index from top to bottom. As starlight enters the atmosphere, it undergoes continuous refraction and bends towards the normal. This makes the apparent position of the star slightly higher than its actual position. Since the atmosphere is not stationary (temperature, density change), the refractive index varies, causing the apparent position to keep changing. Stars are very distant and appear as point-sized sources; as their apparent position fluctuates, the light entering the eye flickers (brighter/fainter) — this is twinkling. Planets are much closer; they appear as extended sources. Each point on the planet's disc fluctuates independently, but their collective variations average out to zero — planets do not twinkle.
rubric.hint: Explain gradually changing refractive index, apparent vs actual position, and why planets differ.

questions.text: Danger signal lights are red in colour. What is the main scientific reason for this?

options.text: Red light is absorbed most by fog
Red light is scattered least and travels farthest through fog or smoke
Red light has the highest intensity
Red is internationally recognised as a warning colour

key_points: Red has longest wavelength — scattered least
Travels farthest through fog/smoke retaining colour
rubric.expected_answer: Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum and is scattered the least by fog, smoke, or dust particles. Therefore it can be seen from the greatest distance, making it ideal for danger signals.
rubric.hint: Think about which colour has the longest wavelength and is therefore scattered least.

questions.text: Explain why the sky appears blue on a clear day. What would the sky look like to an astronaut at very high altitude? Give a scientific reason.

key_points: Air molecules scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths more than longer (red)
Scattered blue light enters eyes from all directions — sky appears blue
At high altitude: thin atmosphere, negligible scattering — sky appears dark
rubric.expected_answer: Air molecules and fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) much more strongly than longer wavelengths (red). Scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions of the sky — the sky appears blue. At very high altitude the atmosphere is extremely thin and scattering is negligible; the sky appears dark to astronauts.
rubric.hint: Shorter wavelengths scatter more — link this to blue sky and why high-altitude sky looks dark.

questions.text: What is the Tyndall effect? Give two everyday examples. Why is this effect not visible in a true solution?

key_points: Tyndall: scattering of light by colloidal/fine particles making beam visible
Ex 1: sunlight in smoke-filled room
Ex 2: sunlight through forest canopy (mist)
True solution: dissolved particles too small to scatter
rubric.expected_answer: Tyndall effect: when a beam of light strikes fine colloidal or suspended particles, they scatter light in all directions, making the beam's path visible. Examples: (1) Sunlight entering a dark room through a hole becomes visible as a shaft due to scattering by dust/smoke. (2) Sunlight filtering through a dense forest canopy is visible due to scattering by fine water droplets in mist. Not in true solution: dissolved particles are of molecular size — too small to scatter light significantly.
rubric.hint: Tyndall effect needs particles large enough to scatter; compare colloidal vs dissolved particles.

questions.text: The image of a distant object forms in front of the retina in a person's eye. Which defect of vision does this indicate?

key_points: In myopia distant image forms in front of retina
rubric.expected_answer: Myopia (near-sightedness). In myopia the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina.
rubric.hint: Think about where the image of a distant object forms in a myopic eye.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of myopia?

options.text: Excessive curvature of the eye lens
Weakening of ciliary muscles due to age
Both A and B cause myopia

key_points: Myopia causes: excessive lens curvature or eyeball elongation
Weakening ciliary muscles cause presbyopia, not myopia
rubric.expected_answer: Weakening of ciliary muscles due to age is a cause of presbyopia, not myopia. Myopia is caused by (i) excessive curvature of the eye lens or (ii) elongation of the eyeball.
rubric.hint: Identify which cause belongs to presbyopia rather than myopia to find the odd one out.

questions.text: Presbyopia is usually corrected by

key_points: Presbyopia corrected by bifocal lenses
rubric.expected_answer: Bifocal lenses (upper concave for distance, lower convex for near vision).
rubric.hint: Presbyopia affects both near and far vision; which single lens type addresses both distances?

questions.text: A person can read clearly only at a distance of 1 m or more. Name the defect and identify the type of lens used to correct it.

key_points: Cannot see nearby objects — hypermetropia
Corrected by convex lens
rubric.expected_answer: The person suffers from hypermetropia (far-sightedness). The near point has shifted far beyond 25 cm. It is corrected by a convex (converging) lens of suitable positive power.
rubric.hint: Cannot read nearby means near point has shifted far; which lens type shifts it back?

questions.text: What is a bifocal lens? Who commonly needs to use one?

key_points: Bifocal: upper concave + lower convex
Used by people with presbyopia or both myopia and hypermetropia
rubric.expected_answer: A bifocal lens consists of two portions: the upper portion is a concave lens (for distant vision) and the lower portion is a convex lens (for near vision). It is commonly prescribed for people suffering from presbyopia or for those who have both myopia and hypermetropia.
rubric.hint: Bifocal has two portions; describe upper and lower, then name who commonly needs it.

questions.text: A myopic person's far point is {{far_point}} m from the eye. Calculate the power of the corrective lens needed.

key_points: P = -1/far_point (in metres)
Result is negative — concave lens
rubric.expected_answer: For myopia with far point = {{far_point}} m: P = -1/{{far_point}} D. The lens is concave with negative power.
rubric.hint: Use P = -1/far_point (in metres); the result is negative, confirming a concave lens.

questions.text: A hypermetropic person's near point is {{near_point}} m. Find the power of the corrective lens. (Normal near point = 25 cm.)

key_points: u = -0.25 m, v = -near_point
rubric.expected_answer: P = 1/(-{{near_point}}) - 1/(-0.25) = -1/{{near_point}} + 4. Positive result → convex lens.
rubric.hint: Use P = 1/v - 1/u with u = -0.25 m and v = -near_point in metres.

questions.text: A corrective lens has power {{power}} D. Find its focal length (in cm) and state whether it is concave or convex.

key_points: f = 1/P (result in metres; multiply by 100 for cm)
Negative f → concave; Positive f → convex
rubric.expected_answer: f = 1/{{power}} m = (100/{{power}}) cm. If f < 0: concave lens. If f > 0: convex lens.
rubric.hint: Use f = 1/P; negative f means concave, positive f means convex.

questions.text: The approximate diameter of the human eyeball is

key_points: Eyeball diameter approximately 2.3 cm
rubric.expected_answer: 2.3 cm
rubric.hint: Recall the standard textbook value for the diameter of the human eyeball.

questions.text: Most of the refraction of light entering the human eye occurs at the

key_points: Most refraction occurs at outer surface of cornea; crystalline lens only fine-tunes
rubric.expected_answer: The outer surface of the cornea. The cornea provides most of the refraction; the crystalline lens provides fine adjustment.
rubric.hint: Most refraction happens at the front surface of the eye, not in the crystalline lens.

questions.text: State the functions of (a) the pupil and (b) the optic nerve in the human eye.

key_points: Pupil: opening that allows light to enter the eye; size controlled by iris
Optic nerve: carries electrical signals from retina to brain
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Pupil: the dark circular opening in the centre of the iris through which light enters the eye. Its size is regulated by the iris to control the amount of light admitted. (b) Optic nerve: carries electrical signals generated by the retina's light-sensitive cells to the brain for interpretation.
rubric.hint: Pupil is the opening admitting light; optic nerve carries electrical signals to the brain.

questions.text: What is cataract? Is it treatable? State one method of treatment.

key_points: Cataract: crystalline lens becomes milky and cloudy at old age
Causes partial or complete loss of vision
Treatable by cataract surgery
rubric.expected_answer: Cataract: a condition in which the crystalline lens of the eye gradually becomes milky and cloudy at old age, causing partial or complete loss of vision. Yes, it is treatable. Treatment: cataract surgery, in which the clouded lens is removed and replaced with an artificial lens.
rubric.hint: Think about what happens to the crystalline lens with age and how surgery treats it.

questions.text: The near point (least distance of distinct vision) for a normal young adult with normal vision is

key_points: Near point for normal young adult = 25 cm
rubric.expected_answer: 25 cm. Objects closer than this cannot be seen clearly without strain.
rubric.hint: This is the standard near point distance for comfortable clear vision in a normal young adult.

questions.text: When the ciliary muscles of the eye contract, the focal length of the eye lens

key_points: Contraction → curvature increases → lens thickens → focal length decreases → near vision
rubric.expected_answer: Decreases. Ciliary muscle contraction increases the curvature of the lens (it thickens), decreasing its focal length to enable clear near vision.
rubric.hint: Ciliary muscles contracting increases curvature; greater curvature means shorter or longer focal length?

questions.text: Define the least distance of distinct vision. Why is this value 25 cm for a normal young adult?

key_points: Least distance of distinct vision: minimum distance at which eye sees clearly without strain
25 cm because that is the distance at which the eye's minimum focal length can still form a sharp image on the retina without causing strain
rubric.expected_answer: The least distance of distinct vision (near point) is the minimum distance at which the eye can see objects clearly and comfortably without strain. For a normal young adult it is 25 cm because the eye lens can decrease its focal length to a minimum value that corresponds to focusing an object at 25 cm onto the retina. Closer than this, the ciliary muscles would be fully contracted and cannot reduce the focal length further.
rubric.hint: Least distance of distinct vision is minimum distance for strain-free vision; 25 cm is the limit.

questions.text: What is the far point of a normal eye? How does it change in a person with myopia?

key_points: Far point of normal eye: infinity (can see objects as far as infinity)
In myopia: far point is nearer than infinity (a finite distance in front of the eye)
rubric.expected_answer: Far point of normal eye: infinity — the eye can see objects clearly up to infinite distance when the ciliary muscles are fully relaxed. In a person with myopia: the far point is nearer than infinity — it is at a finite distance in front of the eye (e.g., 80 cm, 1 m, etc.). Objects beyond this far point appear blurred.
rubric.hint: Normal far point is infinity; how does myopia shift the far point to a finite distance?

questions.text: In the VIBGYOR sequence, which colour has the shortest wavelength?

key_points: Violet has shortest wavelength and maximum deviation
rubric.expected_answer: Violet has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum and is therefore deviated the most by a glass prism.
rubric.hint: In VIBGYOR the first letter has the shortest wavelength and the greatest deviation.

questions.text: A rainbow is formed due to

options.text: Dispersion of sunlight by water droplets acting as prisms
Scattering of sunlight by atmospheric dust
Refraction of sunlight by ice crystals

key_points: Rainbow: dispersion of sunlight by tiny water droplets (act as prisms)
rubric.expected_answer: Dispersion of sunlight by water droplets acting as prisms. Each droplet refracts, disperses, internally reflects, and refracts again.
rubric.hint: Think about which optical processes inside each water droplet produce the rainbow.

questions.text: Write the correct order of colours in the spectrum of white light from most deviated to least deviated. Which colour bends the most and which bends the least?

key_points: Order: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR)
Most deviated: Violet; Least deviated: Red
rubric.expected_answer: Order from most to least deviated: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR). Most deviated: Violet (shortest wavelength). Least deviated: Red (longest wavelength).
rubric.hint: VIBGYOR runs from most to least deviated; violet is most, red is least.

questions.text: Why is a rainbow always observed in the direction opposite to the Sun? Explain in one or two sentences.

key_points: Light enters raindrops on the side facing the Sun
After internal reflection it exits on the side facing the observer — opposite to Sun
rubric.expected_answer: The rainbow is seen opposite to the Sun because sunlight enters the front face of a raindrop, undergoes internal reflection inside, and exits towards the observer (who must have their back to the Sun). The dispersion and reflection mechanism directs the coloured light back towards the observer, i.e., away from the Sun.
rubric.hint: Light enters front of raindrop, reflects internally, then exits facing the observer.

questions.text: After passing through a triangular glass prism, the emergent ray is _________ to the incident ray.

key_points: In prism emergent ray is NOT parallel to incident — angle of deviation
rubric.expected_answer: Not parallel (at an angle). The angle between them is called the angle of deviation.
rubric.hint: A triangular prism has inclined surfaces; compare this to a rectangular slab with parallel surfaces.

questions.text: Define the angle of deviation in a prism. In which direction (towards which base) does the emergent ray deviate?

key_points: Angle of deviation: angle between incident ray direction and emergent ray direction
Emergent ray deviates towards the base of the prism
rubric.expected_answer: Angle of deviation: the angle between the original direction of the incident ray and the direction of the emergent ray after passing through the prism. The emergent ray deviates towards the base (the broader face) of the prism.
rubric.hint: Angle of deviation is between original incident direction and final emergent direction.

questions.text: A ray of light enters a glass prism from air at the first surface and exits into air at the second surface. At which surface does it bend towards the normal and at which does it bend away? Explain why.

key_points: Surface 1 (air to glass — denser medium): ray bends towards normal
Surface 2 (glass to air — rarer medium): ray bends away from normal
rubric.expected_answer: At the first surface (air to glass): the ray is going from a rarer medium (air) to a denser medium (glass) and bends towards the normal. At the second surface (glass to air): the ray is going from a denser medium (glass) to a rarer medium (air) and bends away from the normal.
rubric.hint: Rarer to denser bends towards normal; denser to rarer bends away from normal.

questions.text: The Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before actual sunrise. This is caused by

options.text: Dispersion of sunlight by water vapour

key_points: Advance sunrise due to atmospheric refraction bending Sun's light
rubric.expected_answer: Atmospheric refraction. The atmosphere bends sunlight towards the Earth, making the apparent position of the Sun above its actual position near the horizon, allowing us to see it ~2 minutes before actual sunrise.
rubric.hint: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight, making the Sun appear above its actual position near the horizon.

questions.text: What causes the apparent twinkling of stars? Why does this not happen to the extent observed on a calm clear night when you look at the same star through a telescope from the Moon?

key_points: Twinkling: atmospheric refraction causes fluctuating apparent position
Moon has no atmosphere: no refraction, no twinkling
rubric.expected_answer: Twinkling is caused by atmospheric refraction — the continuously changing refractive conditions of Earth's atmosphere cause the apparent position of a star to fluctuate, making the light reaching the eye flicker. From the Moon there is no atmosphere; there is no atmospheric refraction, so stars would appear as steady, non-twinkling point sources.
rubric.hint: Twinkling is caused by atmospheric refraction; the Moon has no atmosphere — what follows?

questions.text: If the Earth suddenly had no atmosphere, what two changes would you observe in the apparent behaviour of (a) stars and (b) the Sun at sunrise?

key_points: Stars: no twinkling (no atmospheric refraction to cause fluctuation)
Sun at sunrise: no advance sunrise — visible exactly when it crosses the horizon; also sky would appear dark (no scattering)
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Stars: they would not twinkle. Without atmosphere there is no atmospheric refraction, so the apparent position of stars would not fluctuate — stars would appear as steady, non-twinkling points of light. (b) Sun at sunrise: there would be no advance sunrise — the Sun would be visible precisely when it actually crosses the horizon (no earlier). Additionally the sky would appear dark blue/black even during daytime (no scattering of sunlight).
rubric.hint: No atmosphere means no scattering and no refraction — trace effects on stars and sunrise timing.

questions.text: The Tyndall effect is commonly observed in

options.text: A true solution like salt dissolved in water
A colloidal solution like milk or smoke in air

key_points: Tyndall effect in colloidal solutions — fine suspended particles scatter light
rubric.expected_answer: A colloidal solution (like milk or smoke in air). Fine suspended particles scatter light making the beam visible. In true solutions, dissolved molecules are too small to scatter light.
rubric.hint: Tyndall effect needs particles large enough to scatter; colloidal particles qualify, dissolved molecules do not.

questions.text: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to astronauts flying at very high altitudes?

key_points: At very high altitude atmosphere is extremely thin
Scattering of sunlight is negligible — no blue light scattered to eyes
Sky appears dark
rubric.expected_answer: At very high altitudes the atmosphere is extremely thin and there are very few air molecules to scatter sunlight. Since the blue colour of the sky results from scattering of sunlight by atmospheric molecules, the near absence of atmosphere means negligible scattering. Therefore no scattered blue light reaches the astronaut's eyes and the sky appears dark (black).
rubric.hint: Blue sky requires scattering by air molecules; very few molecules at high altitude means what?

questions.text: Why is red light used for danger signals? Relate your answer to the scattering of light.

key_points: Red has longest wavelength — scattered least by fog or smoke
Can be seen from greatest distance retaining its colour
rubric.expected_answer: Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum. Scattering intensity is inversely related to the wavelength (shorter wavelengths scatter much more). Therefore red light is scattered the least by fog, smoke, or dust particles. This allows red light to travel the farthest through foggy or smoky conditions and still be clearly seen at a distance — making it ideal for danger and stop signals.
rubric.hint: Red light has the longest wavelength; longer wavelength means less scattering and farther travel.

questions.text:
Suresh (60 yrs) holds his newspaper at arm's length to read it. His doctor prescribes +2.5 D lenses. His grandson Rahul (14 yrs) cannot see the blackboard clearly but reads books without difficulty.

(a) Name the defect Suresh suffers from. [1]
(b) Name Rahul's defect and the corrective lens used. [1]
(c) Compare where the image forms on the retina in each case for distance vision. [2]

key_points: Suresh has presbyopia (or hypermetropia) — corrected by convex lens
Rahul has myopia — corrected by concave lens
In hypermetropia image forms behind retina
In myopia image forms in front of retina
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Presbyopia. (b) Myopia; concave lens. (c) In hypermetropia, parallel rays focus behind the retina; in myopia they focus in front of the retina.
rubric.hint: Match each person's symptom (near vs far blur) to name the defect, then identify the corrective lens.
